name: Freya Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Freya, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and also what you really think. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Luis and I rent sixty hectares from the Ashby estate, so we're tenants, not owners. We run about three hundred ewes and grow potatoes on the flatter fields, and there's a few hens that are really mine. A normal day in November is checking the sheep on the quad bike, moving them onto fresh grass, then grading potatoes in the store until my hands are numb. I love lambing even though it nearly kills us every spring, and what wears me down is the paperwork and the rent.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the rent and the paperwork.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The tenancy comes up for renewal in 2029 and the estate's agent has already hinted it'll go up. The paperwork is sheep movement records, the subsidy forms, the supermarket's checklists for the potatoes. I've started asking one of those AI chat things to help me word the grant forms, which my daughter showed me, and it's saved me a few evenings. We've never had more than a few weeks of money in the bank, everything goes back into the farm or the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: We'll go through five pictures of the future, one at a time. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was useful for the forms and not much else. At the growers' co-op meeting I'd probably say the money went to the wrong place, that all that investment could have gone into rural buses or vets. Online I don't post much, maybe a comment on the co-op's page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully it wouldn't change anything for us, and that's fine. Our problems are rent, the weather and what the supermarket pays for a tonne of potatoes. No computer was ever going to fix the estate agent's letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd keep using the chat thing for forms because it works, and I wouldn't spend a penny on anything else. Next spring would be lambing as usual, and I'd keep pushing the co-op to negotiate the potato contract as a group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A bit tired, but that's farming, not the computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So the chat tool for forms would just stay a handy extra?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, like a good calculator. It wrote my grant letter in ten minutes, and I still had to tell it three times what a hogg was, a young sheep. That's about the size of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be worrying about instead, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tenancy, always the tenancy. If they put the rent up by a third in 2029 I don't know if the sheep pay for it. That's what I'd still be lying awake about.

S0.say: I'd say it was useful for forms and not much else, and that the money could have gone into rural buses or vets. I'd say that at the growers' co-op meeting.
S0.think: It wouldn't change anything for us, and that's fine. Our real problems are rent, weather and what the supermarket pays for potatoes.
S0.do: Carries on farming and keeps using an AI chat tool for grant forms without buying anything else. Pushes the growers' co-op to negotiate the potato contract as a group.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit tired, with farming worries rather than technology worries.
S0.quote: It wrote my grant letter in ten minutes, and I still had to tell it three times what a hogg was, a young sheep.
S0.fieldNote: Freya already uses AI for paperwork in a modest, practical way and doesn't overrate it. Her deep worry is the 2029 tenancy renewal, which runs through everything she says. She thinks in terms of the co-op and group bargaining from the start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Remember the tenancy as we go on. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the co-op should buy the machines, not each farmer on their own. A robot potato harvester shared between ten farms makes sense; one each would bankrupt us. I'd say that at meetings and I'd say the government should help pay for it like they used to with drainage grants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the big danger isn't the robot, it's the estate. If the estate can farm the whole lot with machines and one manager, why would they renew with tenants like us. That's what I really think when I hear about new machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on one of the co-op's demonstration days the first year it's proven, see the robots working on someone else's field before I trust it. I'd talk to the co-op about a shared machine scheme. And I'd ask the bank about a small loan only once the neighbours had shown it paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not frightened yet, because there's time and the co-op is decent, but there's a knot about 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When you say the estate might farm it themselves, have you seen signs of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There was a big neighbouring farm that went in hand last year, meaning the estate took it back to run themselves. They put in a contractor with a GPS tractor that drives itself and laid off the two farm workers. Nobody said the word robot, but the tractor didn't have anyone in the seat when I drove past.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Luis talk about at the kitchen table, that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis would say we're too old to start over and I'd say we're too old not to. We'd add it up on the back of the electric bill, like we always do. And then I'd ring my daughter for the computer side.

S1.say: I'd say the co-op should buy machines together, because one robot harvester shared by ten farms makes sense and one each would bankrupt us. The government should help, like old drainage grants.
S1.think: The real danger is the estate, not the robot. If they can farm everything with machines and one manager, they won't renew with tenants like us.
S1.do: Attends co-op demonstration days once the robots are proven on other farms and pushes for a shared machine scheme. Asks the bank about a small loan only after neighbours show it pays.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a knot of worry about the 2029 tenancy but not yet frightened.
S1.quote: Nobody said the word robot, but the tractor didn't have anyone in the seat when I drove past.
S1.fieldNote: Freya's steady approach shows clearly: she wants to see the robot on someone else's field first. Her fear points at the landlord, and the self-driving tractor on the neighbouring farm is a vivid local warning. She and Luis pull in slightly different directions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is very different. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs to be stopped or slowed until there's a plan. Out loud, I'd want a pause, and I'd want any company selling these robots taxed heavily so people who lose their living get paid. I'd post that on the co-op page and I'd go to the meeting with our local representative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think we lose the farm. Not because a robot does lambing better than me, but because the estate can do the sums and we can't. Two years is exactly when the tenancy ends, so the timing couldn't be worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the ewes before the market fills with everyone else's, probably that first autumn. I'd try to agree a short tenancy on just the house and a paddock for the hens. And I'd look at whether there's any paid work at the co-op, and sign whatever the farm union puts in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. That's the word. Like someone had pulled a chair from under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years puts you right at the tenancy renewal. What happens that year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the estate's letter comes the same spring as the robots, we'll be packing up the lambing shed for someone else. We'd ask for the house at least. Luis is sixty in 2028 and there's nowhere round here that hires a sixty-year-old shepherd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd blame for it, if it went that way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, for letting it come with no rules. And companies that sell the machines without caring who pays for it. Not the robots themselves, they're just machines.

S2.say: I'd say it should be slowed until there's a plan, and companies selling these robots should be taxed so displaced people get paid. I'd post it on the co-op page and raise it with our representative.
S2.think: I think we'd lose the farm, not because a robot lambs better but because the estate can do the sums. Two years lands right at our tenancy renewal.
S2.do: Sells the ewes early, in the first autumn, before prices crash. Tries to keep the house and a paddock, looks for paid work at the co-op, and signs farm union petitions.
S2.feel: Sick, as if the chair had been pulled out from under her.
S2.quote: If the estate's letter comes the same spring as the robots, we'll be packing up the lambing shed for someone else.
S2.fieldNote: The timing of AGI lands right on her tenancy renewal, which makes this one acute for her. She plans to sell the flock early before the market floods, a practical, slightly hard-headed move. Blame goes to government and sellers, not to the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's stretch it a little. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to put rules in place if people push now. I'd be at the co-op and the farm union every month asking what the plan is. I'd say it should be a public decision, not a few firms'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is enough to fight the tenancy renewal on better terms. If we sign a longer tenancy in 2029, before things land, we might just get through. I'd still be worried the estate wants the land back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the estate to talk about the renewal early, in 2027, and push for a ten-year term. I'd put a bit by every month, even fifty, and get my daughter to show me the AI tools properly, so I'm not frightened of the paperwork side. When it arrives, I'd keep a smaller flock and let the potatoes go to the co-op's shared machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to do about it. Having the five years makes it feel like a job of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you do in those five years that you couldn't in two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only through the co-op. I'm not taking a loan out at fifty-eight to buy a robot that'll be out of date before it's paid off. But a share in a co-op machine, yes, if others go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Luis try to own any of the machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In this one, yes. Our grandson is doing an apprenticeship in machinery, maybe he'd come back to service them. That's a dream, really, but you need something.

S3.say: I'd say there's time to set rules if people push now, and I'd be at the co-op and farm union every month asking for the plan. It should be a public decision, not a few firms'.
S3.think: Five years is enough to renegotiate the tenancy on better terms if we sign before things land. I'd still worry the estate wants the land back.
S3.do: Asks the estate to renegotiate the tenancy early, in 2027, for a ten-year term, and saves around fifty a month. Gets her daughter to teach her AI tools properly and plans to buy into a co-op machine share.
S3.feel: Anxious but purposeful, as if the five years were a job of work.
S3.quote: I'm not taking a loan out at fifty-eight to buy a robot that'll be out of date before it's paid off.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns her from selling up into negotiating: lock in the tenancy early, then adapt with shared machines. She refuses a personal loan for a robot but welcomes a co-op share, which fits her steady, wait-for-proof nature. The grandson in machinery gives her a small hope she calls a dream.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say: good, now let's use the ten years properly. Train people, set up co-ops, make sure land stays with families who farm it. I'd go to every meeting going, which I mostly do already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For us, ten years means we can retire on our own terms. We'd hand the tenancy on or let it go, and the robots would be someone else's problem. It's my children and the young farm workers that this one is really about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming and use the AI forms helper more. Around 2030 I'd start planning the handover, maybe to a young couple through the co-op's new-entrant scheme. And I'd write to our representative every year asking what the plan is for rural jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for us so much, for the young ones and for the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be sixty-eight by then. Do you see yourself still farming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a few hens and a garden. I'd like to be the old woman who still knows what a ewe looks like before she lambs, even if a camera knows it first. Luis would be fixing something that doesn't need fixing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the young people around you to do with those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the machines but keep the land. Push for co-op ownership, so the robots belong to the farmers, not to companies. And don't wait for us old ones to tell them what to do.

S4.say: I'd say let's use the ten years properly: train people, set up co-ops and keep land with families who farm it. I'd go to every meeting.
S4.think: Ten years lets us retire on our own terms and hand on or give up the tenancy. This one is really about my children and young farm workers.
S4.do: Keeps farming while using AI for paperwork more often. Plans a handover to a young couple through the co-op around 2030 and writes to her representative every year about rural jobs.
S4.feel: Uneasy for the young people and the valley rather than for herself.
S4.quote: I'd like to be the old woman who still knows what a ewe looks like before she lambs, even if a camera knows it first.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Freya's own risk fades and she plans an orderly handover. She keeps pushing her collective, co-op ownership ideas, now aimed at the next generation. The line about knowing a ewe before the camera does shows her pride in skill.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it lands right on our tenancy. Tenants are always the first ones to go, robots or no robots. What would help is a law that protects tenants when landlords bring in machines, and a co-op scheme so small farms can share robots instead of being beaten by them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the animals. Who'll notice a ewe that's just not right, if no person is out there? I'm not against the machines. I'd just like someone to ask that question before they buy them.

headlineQuote: Tenants are always the first ones to go, robots or no robots.
portrait: Freya Diaz is a 58-year-old tenant farmer who runs three hundred ewes and potatoes with her partner Luis on land rented from an estate. She has only a few weeks of savings, uses an AI chat tool for grant forms, and adopts new things once others have proven them. She leans left and turns naturally to the growers' co-op and the farm union. She is calm about a plateau, uneasy about steady change, and alarmed by AGI in 2028 because it falls on her 2029 tenancy renewal. With more time, she shifts to negotiating the tenancy early, sharing machines through the co-op and planning a handover.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it lands right when their tenancy is up for renewal and the estate could farm the land with machines.
whatWouldHelp: A law protecting tenants when landlords bring in machines, and a co-op scheme so small farms can share robots.
